title: Start here: how to use this compendium and find your own method
introHtml: This compendium collects the study techniques and habits that learning research supports best, explained in plain words with examples from many fields. It is written for any student: at school, at university, in a training programme or teaching yourself, whether you study languages, law, history, maths, physics, programming, music, economics or medicine. You do not need to read it from start to finish. Skim "How learning works" first (it explains why the techniques work), glance at the time-cost table to see what each technique costs, then pick two or three techniques to try. The section below shows you how to test them on yourself so you end up with a method that fits you, not someone else.

items.title: Finding your method: how to experiment and track what works
items.leadHtml:
Treat finding a study method like a small experiment: try one change at a time, measure it honestly, and keep what works. The aim is a method that suits you and that you enjoy enough to keep using.

Most students choose methods by feel, and feel is a poor guide. In one survey of university students, about 84% listed re-reading as a study strategy and only about 11% listed testing themselves, even though self-testing works much better (Karpicke, Butler & Roediger 2009). The steps below replace "it felt productive" with evidence you collect yourself.

items.title: Step 1: Start from a strong default
items.leadHtml: Begin with retrieval and spacing (blank-page recall, flashcards, questions). Adjust from there rather than starting from scratch.

parts.why: Decades of research agree that pulling information out of memory, at growing intervals, is the most reliable base for almost any subject. Starting there is like a new cook starting from a tested recipe: you can change the spices later, but you are not inventing bread from nothing.
parts.how: For each study block, read or watch once, then close the source and recall (write, sketch or say it). Turn the key facts into a few flashcards or questions. Review them on later days.

examples.simple: A secondary-school student learning French vocabulary reads the list once, covers the French column, and tries to write each word from the English. Missed words go on cards for tomorrow.
examples.nontrivial: A law student starts with the default for contract law (recall the elements of each doctrine, then cards for case names), and only later adds case-comparison tables once she sees that confusing similar cases is her main error.

items.title: Step 2: Change one thing at a time
items.leadHtml: For example, try concept maps instead of flashcards for one subject for one or two weeks.

parts.why: If you change three things at once (new app, new time of day, new method) and your results improve, you will not know which change helped. Scientists hold everything else fixed so the one thing they vary can show its effect, and the same logic works for you.
parts.how: Write down the one change you are testing ("concept maps instead of cards for biochemistry"). Keep your time of day, place and total minutes roughly the same as before.

examples.simple: A history student keeps everything the same but swaps "re-read the chapter" for "blank-page timeline from memory" for two weeks.
examples.nontrivial: A programmer learning a new framework tests "build a tiny project after each tutorial" against "follow the tutorial and take notes". He uses the same tutorial series for both so the content is not the hidden difference, and alternates the methods across similar lessons.

items.title: Step 3: Give it enough time
items.leadHtml: At least 5 sessions over 1 to 2 weeks. Every new method feels awkward at first.

parts.why: The first few sessions measure how unfamiliar the method is, not how good it is. Think of switching to a new keyboard layout: you type slower for days before you type faster. Effortful methods like recall also feel worse than re-reading even when they work better, so a one-day trial is biased against them.
parts.how: Put the trial dates in your calendar. Decide in advance that you will not judge the method before session 5.

examples.simple: A student trying Anki for a geography course feels slow on day 1 and day 2, but by day 6 reviews take half the time and recall is clearly better.
examples.nontrivial: A music student trying to learn a piece by memorising it in small sections from the end backwards finds the first week frustrating. By the second week she notices the endings she used to stumble on are now the most secure part, a benefit she would never have seen in a two-day trial.

items.title: Step 4: Rate every session
items.leadHtml: How much did I recall the next day (1 to 5)? How much did I enjoy it? How focused was I? How much effort did it take?

parts.why: Memory of how a week went is vague and biased by the last session. A quick rating after each session builds a small data set. The next-day recall question matters most, because it measures learning after some forgetting, not the warm glow straight after study.
parts.how: Keep a note or a spreadsheet with one row per session. Rate enjoyment, focus and effort at the end of the session; rate recall at the start of the next day, after a quick 2-minute test on yesterday's material.

examples.simple: A biology student ends each session with three numbers in her phone's notes app: enjoy 4, focus 3, effort 4. Next morning she adds recall 3.
examples.nontrivial: An economics student notices that his "effort" score is high on days his recall is also high, and low on days recall is poor. That pattern tells him that sessions that feel easy are the ones to be suspicious of.

items.title: Step 5: Use objective signals too
items.leadHtml: Question-bank scores, how many gaps appear in blank-page recall, and how well topics hold up at the 7-day review.

parts.why: Ratings are still feelings. Objective signals are harder to fool yourself with: a score or a count of gaps does not care how fluent the page felt. Students are generally overconfident after re-reading and better calibrated after testing, so the objective signal is your reality check.
parts.how: Pick one or two numbers you can collect without extra effort: percentage correct on practice questions, number of items missed on a blank-page recall, or number of flashcards you failed at the 7-day review.

examples.simple: A maths student counts how many of 10 practice problems he solves without looking at the worked solution.
examples.nontrivial: A medical student tracks question-bank scores per topic and sees that cardiology is at 75% but drops to 55% when the questions are mixed with respiratory topics. The method she used produced knowledge that only works when she already knows which chapter a question comes from, so she adds interleaving.

items.title: Step 6: Decide: keep, tweak or drop
items.leadHtml: Keep what scores well on both recall and enjoyment. Tweak what has good recall but feels boring. Drop what you enjoy but can't recall.

parts.why: A method has to pass two tests: it must work (recall) and you must actually keep doing it (enjoyment). A brilliant method you abandon after a week is worth less than a good method you use every day. This rule makes the decision explicit instead of drifting.
parts.how:
1. Average the recall and enjoyment ratings for the trial.
  2. High recall and high enjoyment: keep.
  3. High recall, low enjoyment: tweak the format (shorter sessions, a study partner, a different app, standing up).
  4. Low recall, high enjoyment: drop it as a main method; keep it as a warm-up if you like it.
  5. Low on both: drop.

examples.simple: A language learner loves watching films with subtitles but recalls few new words the next day. He keeps films for Friday evenings and does cards on weekdays.
examples.nontrivial: A physics student finds blank-page recall very effective but dull. Instead of dropping it, she tweaks it: she explains the derivation aloud while walking, and records herself. Recall stays high and enjoyment rises from 2 to 4.

items.title: Step 7: Match methods to content
items.leadHtml: One person may end up with flashcards for vocabulary, drawing for processes and worked problems for maths.

parts.why: Different material has different structure. Arbitrary facts (dates, vocabulary, drug names) need repetition; processes need a picture of the sequence; skills need practice. One method rarely fits everything, the way one tool does not fit every screw.
parts.how: Sort each course's content into rough types: facts, processes, concepts, skills. Run your trials per type, and write down the winner for each.

examples.simple: A chemistry student uses cards for the names of functional groups and practice problems for reaction mechanisms.
examples.nontrivial: A medicine student ends up with flashcards for pharmacology, drawing for physiology and cases for pathology. A law student in the same building uses cards for case names, flowcharts for procedure, and essay outlines for policy debates. Both arrived there by testing, not by copying each other.

items.title: Step 8: Review monthly
items.leadHtml: Methods that worked for one course or year may need to change for the next.

parts.why: Your material, your workload and your skill as a learner all change. A method that suited first-year anatomy (lots of names) may not suit clinical years (lots of reasoning), and what suited beginner Spanish (vocabulary) may not suit advanced Spanish (fluency and nuance).
parts.how: Once a month, spend 15 minutes with your session log. Ask: what is my weakest subject or content type now, and which method am I using there? Pick one new experiment for the coming month.

examples.simple: A student moving from introductory to intermediate statistics notices his card-heavy method no longer helps with choosing the right test, and adds mixed practice problems.
examples.nontrivial: An adult learning to code notices that tutorials worked well for the first three months but her progress has stalled. Her log shows high enjoyment but falling recall of how to structure programs on her own. She switches to building small projects from a blank file, which feels slower but shows steady gains.

items.title: Things worth tracking
items.leadHtml:
Each signal below answers a different question. Together they tell you whether a method works, whether you will keep doing it, and where to spend your next hour.

  • Study sessions: date, course, method, minutes, recall rating, enjoyment, focus. This is the core of the experiment. Minutes let you compare methods per unit of time, not just per session. Enjoyment and focus predict whether you will keep going. The recall rating should be taken the next day: same-day recall mostly measures what is still in short-term memory, and a feeling of fluency right after study is a poor predictor of what you will know in a week.
  • Topics: when learned, review dates, how each review went. This shows the shape of your own forgetting. If a topic is solid at day 3 but shaky at day 14, your gaps between reviews are too long for that kind of material. If reviews are always easy, you can stretch the gaps and save time.
  • Question scores per topic over time. The most objective measure you have, and the closest to an exam. A rising line means the method is working for that topic. A flat line despite many hours means time is going in but not sticking. Compare scores on blocked sets (one topic) with mixed sets: a big drop on mixed sets means you know the content but cannot yet tell when to use it.
  • Weekly reflection: what worked, what didn't, one change for next week. Numbers tell you what happened; reflection tells you why. "Recall was low on Wednesday" becomes useful once you note "I studied after a 9-hour shift". Limiting yourself to one change keeps the experiment clean (step 2).
  • Wins and small milestones. These are not vanity. Seeing progress is one of the strongest drivers of motivation, and a list of wins is the evidence you need on a bad day that the method does work.

items.title: A worked example: one 2-week experiment
items.leadHtml:
This is an illustration with made-up but realistic numbers, not data from a study.

Maya is a second-year psychology student. She usually re-reads her notes and highlights them. She wants to know whether blank-page recall works better for her. She picks two similar topics from the same module, each with about the same number of pages and the same lecturer: "Memory" and "Attention".

Setup.

  • Topic A (Memory): her usual method, re-read and highlight, 40 minutes per session.
  • Topic B (Attention): read once, then blank-page recall and fill gaps in a second colour, 40 minutes per session.
  • Five sessions per topic over 2 weeks, alternating days so neither topic always gets the "fresh" morning slot.
  • After each session: enjoyment, focus and effort (1 to 5). Next morning: a 2-minute quiz of 5 questions on yesterday's material, scored as recall (1 to 5).
  • On day 14: a 20-question practice quiz on each topic, from the module's question bank.

Results (averages over 5 sessions).

SignalA: Re-read + highlightB: Blank-page recall
How well I felt I knew it (end of session)4.43.0
Next-day recall (1 to 5)2.63.8
Enjoyment3.43.0
Focus2.84.0
Effort2.04.0
Day-14 quiz (20 questions)11/20 (55%)16/20 (80%)

What Maya learns.

  1. Her feeling of knowing was highest for the method that produced the least learning. That gap is the fluency illusion in her own data.
  2. Blank-page recall was harder (effort 4.0) and slightly less enjoyable, but it held up the next day and at two weeks.
  3. Focus was much higher with recall, because she could not drift while producing answers.

Decision. Keep blank-page recall as her main method. Because enjoyment was a little lower, tweak it: she will do the recall with a friend once a week and compare pages. She keeps a 5-minute skim of her notes as a warm-up, not as the main study. Next month's experiment: adding flashcards for the definitions she keeps missing.

Limits. Two topics are never perfectly equal, and one student is not a study. If Maya wanted more confidence she could swap the methods for the next two topics and see if the pattern repeats.
